{{Short description|Topic in applied statistics}} 
'''Economic statistics''' is a topic in [[applied statistics]] and [[applied economics]] that concerns the [[data collection|collection]], processing, compilation, dissemination, and [[data analysis|analysis]] of [[economic data]]. It is closely related to [[business statistics]] and [[econometrics]].<ref name="Becker Greene pp. 169–182">{{cite journal | last1=Becker | first1=William E | last2=Greene | first2=William H | title=Teaching Statistics and Econometrics to Undergraduates | journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives | publisher=American Economic Association | volume=15 | issue=4 | date=2001-11-01 | issn=0895-3309 | doi=10.1257/jep.15.4.169 | pages=169–182| doi-access=free }}</ref> It is also common to call the data themselves "economic statistics", but for this usage, "economic data" is the more common term.

== Overview ==
The data of concern to economic statistics may include those of an [[economy]] within a region, country, or group of countries. Economic statistics may also refer to a subtopic of [[official statistics]] for data produced by official organizations (e.g. [[List of national and international statistical services|national statistical services]], intergovernmental organizations such as [[United Nations]], [[European Union]] or [[OECD]], [[central bank]]s, and ministries).

Analyses within economic statistics both make use of and provide the empirical data needed in economic research, whether descriptive or [[econometric]]. They are a key input for decision making as to [[economic policy]]. The subject includes statistical analysis of topics and problems in [[microeconomics]], [[macroeconomics]], [[business]], [[finance]], [[economic forecasting|forecasting]], [[data quality]], and [[Policy analysis|policy evaluation]].<ref>• Charles J. Bullock, 1919. [https://www.jstor.org/stable/1928753 "Prefatory Statement,"] ''Review of Economic Statistics'', 1(1), [unnumbered page].<br/>&nbsp;&nbsp; • [[Arnold Zellner]], 1983. "Editorial Statement," ''Journal of Business and Economic Statistics'', 1(1), pp. 1-4.<br/>&nbsp;&nbsp; • [[Eric Ghysels]] and Alastair Hall,  2002. "Editors' Introduction to Twentieth Anniversary Commemorative Issue," ''Journal of Business and Economic Statistics'', 20(1), pp. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120721213836/http://pubs.amstat.org/doi/abs/10.1198/073500102753410345?journalCode=jbes|title=1}}-4.</ref> It also includes such considerations as what data to collect in order to quantify some particular aspect of an economy and of how best to collect in any given instance.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Giovannini|first=Enrico|title=Understanding economic statistics : an OECD perspective|date=2008|publisher=OECD|others=Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development|isbn=978-92-64-04698-6|location=Paris|oclc=263693127}}</ref>
